title: China’s Advance in the Bahamas
gist: The author argues China has built a strategically problematic commercial and influence presence in the Bahamas, 80 km from the US, via ports, resorts, Huawei and Hikvision tech, solar and training, which could let Beijing observe or threaten US force deployments.

insights.claim: The Bahamas lie 80 km from the US at their closest, nearer than Cuba, on US military maritime routes the State Department calls the US 'third border,' so Chinese presence matters for US force projection toward the Indo-Pacific.
insights.speaker: R. Evan Ellis
insights.so_what: Expect US policy attention and pressure on Nassau consistent with the December 2025 NSS.

insights.claim: Hutchison operates the Freeport container and cruise terminals and is doing a $100 million modernization with cranes associated with data security concerns.
insights.speaker: R. Evan Ellis
insights.so_what: Port ownership and equipment are focal points for US pressure.

insights.claim: Chow Tai Fook owns the $4.2 billion Baha Mar resort, whose Chinese builder CCA was found by US courts to have caused $845 million in damages; Chinese projects like The Pointe hired 229 Chinese nationals versus 90 Bahamians despite a 70 percent local-hire requirement.
insights.speaker: R. Evan Ellis
insights.so_what: Contract violations show weak Bahamian control over Chinese-run projects.

insights.claim: Huawei supplies the national telecom operator ALIV and BTC, Hikvision provided over 2,000 cameras at Baha Mar, and Chinese firms Sungrow, Kehua and GSL supply solar and storage, giving exposure in sensitive data, surveillance and energy sectors.
insights.speaker: R. Evan Ellis
insights.so_what: Telecom, surveillance and energy dependence is the main security exposure; watch for US pressure on Huawei and Hikvision.

insights.claim: Six Royal Bahamas Defense Force personnel trained in Chinese institutions in 2025, China brought about 100 Bahamians to China in the past year, and delegations from both major parties went to Beijing in July 2026.
insights.speaker: R. Evan Ellis
insights.so_what: Broad elite cultivation reduces Bahamian political resistance to Chinese projects.

insights.claim: China has courted Bahamian journalists, particularly from The Tribune and Eyewitness News, via paid trips, and many trips produced enthusiastic op-eds on China.
insights.speaker: R. Evan Ellis
insights.so_what: Media cultivation shapes Bahamian public opinion of China.

insights.claim: The Confucius Institute at the University of the Bahamas, begun in 2009 and a full institute since 2012, had trained over 1,000 students by 2019.
insights.speaker: R. Evan Ellis
insights.so_what: Soft-power channel with a long track record.

insights.claim: Though mostly commercial and political rather than military, China's Bahamas presence should draw Washington's attention, and the author expects the administration to act on NSS priorities.
insights.speaker: R. Evan Ellis
insights.so_what: Raises odds of US action targeting Chinese ventures in the Bahamas.
